examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying Expressions in Degrees Using the Sum and Difference Formulas
examples.problem: Express $\cos(x - 60^\circ)$ in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x.$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\cos(u - v) = \cos{u}\cos{v} + \sin{u}\sin{v}
$$

Applying the difference formula for cosine with $u = x$ and $v = 60^\circ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-{60}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{60}^{∘}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Using the fact that $-\frac{11\pi }{12}=\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{5\pi }{4},$
calculate the **exact** value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{11\pi }{12}).$

$\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{11\pi }{12})=$
{{field-1}}
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

Applying the sum formula for cosine with $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $y=\frac{5\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{11\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{5\pi }{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
